titre: The Challenger Deep Flatfish That No One Could Prove
accroche: On January 23, 1960, two men touch the bottom of the Mariana Trench. One of them says he saw a fish, with no photo to establish it.
contenu_vulgarise:
January 23, 1960. The bathyscaphe Trieste, bought by the American Office of Naval Research in 1958 for $267,000, touches the bottom of the Challenger Deep, about 200 miles southwest of Guam. On board are Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh. In the chronology of the US Navy Electronics Laboratory report, the day takes a single line: a successful dive in the Challenger Deep, in 35,800 feet of water, or about 10,900 meters.

## A Corrected Depth

This figure is not the one the onboard instruments first displayed. They indicated 11,521 meters, a value later revised to 10,916 meters. Recent measurements place the deepest point between about 10,911 and 10,994 meters. The difference between raw reading and accepted value thus exceeds 600 meters: a record can be real and its figure unstable. The Trieste itself took nearly five hours to descend, at less than a meter per second, then about twenty minutes on the bottom before coming back up.

## A Witness Without a Camera

On the bottom, the two men stay about twenty minutes. The Trieste carries no camera. As it settles, one of the two men reports having seen, before the stirred-up sediment clouded everything, a small flat fish. The observation goes around the world: life thus apparently exists at the deepest point of the oceans.

Several studies have since sought to rule it out, including a 2012 article by Alan Jamieson and Paul Yancey, titled “On the Validity of the Trieste Flatfish.” Their main concern lies elsewhere: they mostly fear that the observation gives a sensationalist picture of the depths. The strongest ecological argument comes from a separate study, published in 2009 with Alan Jamieson already among the authors: at such depths, fish depend on the detritus and carcasses that fall from above, which organisms in the upper layers will almost all have consumed beforehand. Extrapolations of fish distribution by depth also predict a limit at around 8,500 meters. The explanation judged most likely is that of a flattened sea cucumber, easy to mistake for a flatfish. No one suspects the pilot of having lied.

## What This Says About an Account

The 8,500-meter limit comes from extrapolations, which make poor allowance for exceptions. But the absence of proof counts too: without an image, a testimony, however sincere, does not become a fact. Once doubt is raised, the most quoted sentence of the 1960 dive is an observation that neither side can verify.

carte.punch: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 1960, a fish was reportedly seen. There was no camera.
carte.idee: On January 23, 1960, Piccard and Walsh touch the bottom of the Challenger Deep, at 35,800 feet according to the Navy's log. A flatfish was reportedly glimpsed there; without an image, the observation remains contested and the most likely explanation is a sea cucumber.

quiz.question: Why does the observation of a flatfish at the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 1960 remain contested?
choix: No image establishes it, and food rarely arrives there
The pilot admitted having made up the episode
The Trieste's cracked porthole supposedly made any observation impossible
quiz.explication: The doubt comes from the absence of proof and from ecology: little food reaches the bottom, and models predict a limit for fish at around 8,500 meters. No one accuses the pilot of lying, and flatfish do not live at these depths.

quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry cites the Office of Naval Research's purchase of the Trieste in 1958 for $267,000, a figure distinct from the depth measurements in feet or meters.

Twelve hours, slowed by the stirred-up sediment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the Trieste took nearly five hours to descend, at less than a meter per second, before staying about twenty minutes on the bottom.

choix: No gap, the figure never changed
